topic: 综合模拟二与稳定性检查
grammarFocus: 根据两轮结果检查重复错误，巩固准确表达与稳定句型。
title: Week 50 Listening Simulation: Stability Check
instructions: 本材料为原创模拟练习，非官方雅思试题，也不代表任何正式分数。请先听录音（或阅读录音稿），然后完成四个部分的题目。听力共40题，按顺序排列。每部分10题。单选题请选择最符合原文的完整选项；填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过字数限制。所有解析为中文，证据为英文原文引用。
transcript:
SECTION 1: Social Dialogue

Narrator: You will hear a conversation between a student, Mei, and a housing officer, Mr. Collins, about a room in a shared house. Mei has been looking for accommodation near the university for several weeks, and she found the advertisement on the university noticeboard earlier that morning. She is now calling Mr. Collins to ask for more details and to arrange a viewing.

Mei: Hello, I'm calling about the room advertised on the university noticeboard. Is it still available?

Mr. Collins: Yes, it is. It's a single room in a three-bedroom house on Willow Street. The rent is £420 a month, including bills. That means you won't have to worry about separate payments for electricity, gas, or water. Everything is covered in that monthly amount, so you can budget easily.

Mei: That sounds reasonable. How far is it from the campus?

Mr. Collins: It's about a fifteen-minute walk, or five minutes by bike. There's a bus stop right outside, but the bus only comes every twenty minutes. Many of our tenants cycle, as it's usually the quickest option. The route is quite flat, so it's an easy ride even if you're not a very experienced cyclist.

Mei: OK. What about the other tenants?

Mr. Collins: There are two other tenants at the moment. One is a postgraduate student in engineering, and the other works at the hospital. Both are quiet and tidy, and they have lived there for over a year. They are both quite busy, so the house is usually peaceful during the day.

Mei: Good. Is there a washing machine?

Mr. Collins: Yes, there's a washing machine in the kitchen, and a dryer in the garage. But you need to pay £1 for each use. The money goes towards the electricity, and it keeps things fair for everyone. It's a simple system and we've never had any problems with it.

Mei: I see. And is there a garden?

Mr. Collins: There's a small back garden, but it's shared with the neighbours. You can use it, but you can't have parties there after 10 p.m. The neighbours are friendly, but they value their quiet evenings. During the day, you're welcome to sit outside or hang your washing, as long as you keep the shared space tidy.

Mei: That's fine. When can I see the room?

Mr. Collins: I can show you tomorrow at 2 p.m., or Thursday at 10 a.m. Which is better?

Mei: Tomorrow at 2 p.m. works for me.

Mr. Collins: Great. The address is 14 Willow Street. Please ring the bell for flat 2. It's on the ground floor, so you don't need to climb any stairs. The entrance is on the left side of the building, just past the bike racks.

Mei: Thank you. One more thing—is there a deposit?

Mr. Collins: Yes, it's one month's rent, so £420. You get it back when you leave, as long as the room is in good condition. We also ask tenants to give one month's notice before moving out. That gives us time to find a new tenant and keeps things running smoothly.

Mei: Understood. See you tomorrow.

SECTION 2: Social Monologue

Narrator: You will hear a talk given by a volunteer coordinator at a community centre. The coordinator is speaking to a group of local residents who are interested in getting involved. The talk covers three different volunteer activities and explains how to join the programme.

Speaker: Good morning, everyone. I'm here to tell you about our new volunteer programme at the Riverside Community Centre. We are looking for people to help with three activities: gardening, cooking, and reading with children. Each activity is designed to support different groups in our community, and we welcome volunteers of all ages and backgrounds. Whether you have just an hour a week or more time to give, there is a place for you here.

The gardening group meets every Saturday from 9 to 11 a.m. You don't need any experience—just bring gloves and a willingness to get your hands dirty. We grow vegetables and flowers, and everything we grow is given to local families. Last year, we donated over 200 kilograms of fresh produce, and we hope to do even more this year. The work is physical but very rewarding, and many volunteers say it's a great way to relax after a busy week.

The cooking group meets on Wednesday evenings from 6 to 8 p.m. We prepare simple meals for elderly people in the neighbourhood. You will learn basic cooking skills, and you can take home a portion of what we make. The meals are delivered by another team of volunteers, so your work in the kitchen directly helps people who may struggle to cook for themselves. It's a friendly group, and you'll pick up useful recipes along the way.

The reading programme is on Tuesday afternoons from 3 to 4 p.m. We read stories with children aged 6 to 9. You don't need to be a teacher, but you do need to enjoy reading aloud and be patient. Many of the children are learning English as a second language, so reading together also helps them build confidence. The sessions are relaxed and fun, and the children really look forward to them.

To join, please fill in a form at the front desk. There is no fee, but we ask for a commitment of at least four weeks. This helps us plan ahead and ensures that the people we support see familiar faces. If you are interested, come to our open day next Monday at 10 a.m. in the main hall. You can meet the team and ask questions. Thank you.

SECTION 3: Academic Discussion

Narrator: You will hear a discussion between two students, Anna and Ben, and their tutor, Dr. Patel, about a group presentation on urban transport. They are meeting in Dr. Patel's office to review their progress before the final submission. The tutor offers advice on structure, analysis, and timing.

Dr. Patel: So, Anna and Ben, how is your presentation on urban transport coming along?

Anna: We've done most of the research, but we're not sure how to organise it. We have a lot of information about cycling schemes in different cities.

Ben: Yes, and we found that the results are mixed. For example, in one city, cycling increased by 30% after they built new bike lanes, but in another city, the increase was only 5%.

Dr. Patel: That's interesting. Why do you think there was such a difference?

Anna: We think it depends on how safe people feel. In the city with the 30% increase, they also reduced speed limits and added separate lanes. In the other city, the lanes were just painted on the road, without any barriers. So people didn't feel protected from traffic.

Dr. Patel: Good point. So you could argue that infrastructure design matters more than just the number of lanes. What about the presentation structure?

Ben: We thought we'd start with the benefits of cycling, then compare the two cities, and finish with recommendations.

Dr. Patel: That sounds logical. But remember to include some data on costs. How much did each city spend?

Anna: We have that information. The first city spent €2 million, and the second spent €500,000. But the second city has a much smaller population.

Dr. Patel: So you should compare spending per person, not just total spending. That will make your analysis stronger.

Ben: We hadn't thought of that. We'll add that.

Dr. Patel: Also, make sure you cite your sources clearly. Where did you get the figures?

Anna: From the city councils' annual reports. We'll put the references on the final slide.

Dr. Patel: Good. And try to keep the presentation to 15 minutes, with 5 minutes for questions. I look forward to seeing it next Friday.

SECTION 4: Academic Lecture

Narrator: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of tea. The lecture is part of a series on global trade and cultural exchange. The lecturer traces tea's spread from China to Japan, Europe, and India, and discusses how it became a global drink.

Lecturer: Today I want to talk about the history of tea, focusing on how it spread from China to the rest of the world. Tea was first drunk in China, possibly as early as the Shang dynasty, though the earliest written record dates from the 3rd century CE. Initially, it was used as a medicine, not as an everyday drink. People believed it had healing properties and used it to treat various ailments.

During the Tang dynasty, from 618 to 907, tea became a popular beverage. The government even taxed it, which shows how important it had become. It was during this period that tea was taken to Japan by Buddhist monks, who had studied in China. They brought tea seeds and the custom of drinking tea back with them. The monks used tea in religious ceremonies, and over time it became central to Japanese culture.

Tea reached Europe much later. The Portuguese were the first Europeans to bring tea to Europe in the early 16th century, but it was the Dutch who established the first regular trade in tea, shipping it from China to Amsterdam in 1610. The British initially found tea expensive and it was mainly drunk by the wealthy. However, by the 18th century, it had become a national drink in Britain. The price gradually fell as trade expanded, and tea became part of daily life for ordinary people.

One key development was the introduction of tea to India by the British in the 19th century. They wanted to break the Chinese monopoly on tea. They found that tea could grow well in Assam, and by the end of the 19th century, India was producing large quantities of tea. This shifted the balance of the global tea trade and made tea more widely available.

Today, tea is the most widely consumed drink in the world after water. But the way it is drunk varies greatly. In Britain, people often add milk, while in China, tea is usually drunk without milk. In Japan, green tea is central to the tea ceremony. These differences show how a single product can be adapted to different cultures.

So, in conclusion, tea's journey from China to the world is a story of trade, empire, and cultural exchange. Next week, we will look at the role of the East India Company in more detail.

grammar.title: Stability Check: Avoiding Repeated Errors
grammar.explanation: 本部分帮助你检查两轮练习中常见的重复错误，巩固准确表达和稳定句型。重点包括：主谓一致、时态一致、比较结构、被动语态和介词搭配。请先理解句意，再选择最准确的表达。
grammar.example: The rent is £420 a month, including bills.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The number of volunteers have increased.
The number of volunteers has increased.
A number of volunteers has increased.
The number of volunteers are increasing.
answers: The number of volunteers has increased.
questions.explanation: “the number of + 复数名词”作主语时，谓语用单数。
questions.evidence: The number of volunteers has increased.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I would have known, I would have come.
If I had known, I would have come.
If I knew, I would have come.
If I have known, I would come.
answers: If I had known, I would have come.
questions.explanation: 与过去事实相反的虚拟条件句：if + had done, would have done。
questions.evidence: If I had known, I would have come.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She suggested to go to the museum.
She suggested going to the museum.
She suggested go to the museum.
She suggested that go to the museum.
answers: She suggested going to the museum.
questions.explanation: suggest 后接动名词，不接不定式。
questions.evidence: She suggested going to the museum.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The data was collected by the researchers.
The data were collected by the researchers.
The data collected by the researchers.
The data has collected by the researchers.
answers: The data were collected by the researchers.
questions.explanation: 在学术语境中，data 常作复数，谓语用 were；被动语态结构为 be + 过去分词。
questions.evidence: The data were collected by the researchers.
